name: 24-hour clock, calendar and number formats
plain: Reads 12 or 24 hour clock, first weekday, calendar type and number format.
meaning: Small habit signals that add fingerprint bits: 24 hour clock, Monday start, Hijri or Buddhist calendar.

ios.api_surface: Calendar identifier, 12 or 24 hour cycle (hourCycle iOS 16)

limits.headline: Can see your 12 or 24 hour clock setting, calendar type and number style
limits.user_action: Nothing. It happens when the app shows dates, times or numbers
can: Check for a 12 or 24 hour clock
Find your calendar type and first day of the week
Format numbers and dates the way you expect
cannot: See your calendar events or contacts
Change your clock or calendar settings
Tell who you are from these settings alone, though they add to a device fingerprint

story.what_it_is: An app sees whether you use a 24 hour clock, which day your week starts and your calendar style.
story.for_you: You do not see it. Apps just show dates the way you like them, like 17:30 instead of 5:30 PM. It is a convenience that also tells the app a little about where you may come from.
story.for_makers: Makers need this to format dates and numbers correctly. Ad and anti fraud systems also use the combination as a small clue about a device. It adds only a few bits, but together with other habits it helps pick one phone out of many.

use_cases.example: A flight app shows departure times in 24 hour time because your phone is set that way.
A calendar app starts the week on Monday or Sunday to match your setting.
A running app shows distance and pace with your number format.
A live event in a game shows start times in your own clock style.
A bank app shows amounts with the right decimal and thousands separators.
A tracking script adds clock and calendar to a quiet device profile, which makes two phones easier to tell apart.

story.android_note: Android apps read these through the locale and settings with no prompt.
story.ios_note: iPhone apps read these through the locale with no prompt.
